title: De altitudine columnarum sub proprio pondere corruentium

deep.reconstruction:
Problem served: E510 asks how tall a column can be before it collapses under its own weight. In §6 (previous page) Euler sets the problem up through an imperfection argument. He pins both ends A and B on a vertical line and pushes the middle C sideways with a small horizontal force Cc. He then solves for the slightly bent shape. Self-weight buckling is the limiting case in which a bent equilibrium can survive when that force goes to zero.

On this page (§7–8) he first treats a simpler discrete model. The continuous column is replaced by two rigid bars AC and CB, each of length a and weight M. They are joined at C by a hinge that resists bending through an elastic moment. This is a two-link rigid-bar/rotational-spring model.

Forces in §8:
- each bar's weight M acts at its midpoint;
- the horizontal force C acts at the hinge;
- the hinge stiffness is pictured as a spring Ee joining two points at distance e from C, one on each arm, which tries to straighten them.

Geometry and spring:
- With ∠CAB = ∠CBA = θ, the bend angle at the hinge is ∠ECe = 2θ.
- The spring force is taken proportional to that angle for small θ, giving E·2θ with lever arm ≈ e.
- The restoring moment is therefore 2Eeθ, a linear rotational spring of stiffness k = 2Ee per unit of relative rotation... more precisely M_hinge = Ee·(2θ).
- Dropping the horizontal CO from C gives CO = a sinθ and AO = BO = a cosθ.
- The next page linearises these to CO = aθ and AO = a.

What follows on the next pages: Euler adds the unknown support reactions (horizontal A at A; vertical 2M and horizontal B at B) and writes force and moment equilibrium. This leads to a critical relation between Ee, M, a and C. As C → 0, a nonzero θ is possible only at a critical weight, the discrete analogue of the self-weight buckling load.
errors: No mathematical error on this page. Minor looseness: the 'vis elastica absoluta' E is used without stating its dimensions. The moment 2Eeθ quietly assumes the spring force is proportional to the hinge angle and that its lever arm is e·cosθ ≈ e. Both hold to first order in θ, which is the stated regime.

ideas.what: Replacing a continuous elastic column by rigid links joined by an elastic hinge (rotational spring) to study buckling
ideas.modern_name: Rigid-bar / rotational-spring discrete buckling model (Hencky bar-chain; 'Shanley-type' two-link column used in stability textbooks)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Hencky (1920) for the systematic bar-chain discretisation. The textbook two-link spring column is ubiquitous (Timoshenko, Bažant–Cedolin) and is usually not attributed.
ideas.where_published: E510 itself (Acta Acad. Sci. Imp. Petrop. 1778:I, publ. 1780). Discussed in Truesdell's 1960 survey of Euler's elasticity (Opera omnia II 11/2); exact coverage there unsure.

ideas.what: Studying buckling via a small lateral perturbing force and asking when the deflection persists as the force vanishes
ideas.modern_name: Imperfection / lateral-load approach to the bifurcation load
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler himself in the 1778 column papers; later Southwell (1932) for the experimental plot

ideas.what: Small-angle linearisation of the spring moment and geometry: CO = a sinθ ≈ aθ, hinge angle 2θ

missed.claim: Euler's use of a two-rigid-bar column with an elastic hinge is an early explicit instance of the discrete spring-link buckling model. Here it is applied to the self-weight problem as a stepping stone to the continuum. Histories of the discrete (Hencky) bar-chain model seldom cite Euler 1778 as a precursor. This is a priority/credit note, not a new result.
missed.quote: in medio C eiusmodi iunctura tribuatur, quae cum certo elasticitatis momento flexurae resistat
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Historical precedent for discrete-element and bar-chain models of elastic stability, commonly dated to the 20th century.

deep.surprise_reason: The page sets up a routine two-link, rotational-spring model with small-angle geometry. Its only notable feature is being an early, rarely credited instance of the discrete bar-spring buckling model. The E510 column papers themselves are well known (Truesdell).
transcription_corrections: 'interuallum CE = Ce': the scan shows a smudged 'CE' (OCR-like 'Ch'); the intended reading is CE = Ce.
'ad angulum A C e' is confirmed by the image; the spring is denoted 'elastrum E e'.
